newsitem.title: UK: BBC calls for common digital TV standards.
newsitem.headline: BBC calls for common digital TV standards.

text.p: The British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) on Wednesday repeated a call for the government to set common standards for digitial TV receiver technology and said operators of set-top boxes should licence the system to both broadcasters and manufacturers.

The BBC was responding to the government's proposals for a regulatory regime for the digital technology which is set to revolutionise TV programming with hundreds of channels available plus other services like pay per view and home shopping.

"This is the last chance to create an orderly, open market in digital TV where everyone will benefit," said Patricia Hodgson BBC director of policy and planning. "But the government's latest proposals still risk creating uncertainty for competition and consumer."
As well as increasing the number of channels, digital technology enhances sound and pictures by converting them into binary digits rather than transmitting them as electric signals.

In order to do this, however, a set-top box or decoder is required and this has been the source of controversy as some fear British Sky Broadcasting, in which Rupert Murdoch's News Corp is the biggest shareholder, will dominate the market.
This might mean consumers may need more than one decoder unless there is a common standard.

Hodgson compared BSkyB's position as the "first-mover" in the technology with computer giant Microsoft which had licensed its computer operating technolgy to other manufacturers leading to the dominance of the PC and huge profits for the innovator.
"Nobody is saying that the first-mover shouldn't get a reward."

She acknowledged that the government currently sees as a last resort the BBC's wish that the dominant set-top box operator would be required to licence the technical specification needed by the broadcaster if the operator unreasonably refuses to carry a competitors signals.
"(But this is ) the measure that opened the computer software and telecoms industry in the UK to competition," Hodgson said. "It needs to be in place from the launch of digital broadcasting."
Hodgson said the BBC expects the new regulations to come into effect around the end of January next year.
Currently, it is expected that BSkyB will launch digital satellite services in the Autumn of 1997 while terrestrial service is expected to get under way in the Spring or Summer of 1998.
